objective: Analyzing experiment and testing results to justify a final model recommendation: performance evaluation, diagnostic plots, benchmarking, and requirements validation
secondaryObjectives: Conducting the model design iteration process: design constraints, model selection, literature review, hyperparameter tuning, and experiment tracking
Translating and communicating results: choosing visualizations and reports for executive, domain, and peer audiences while avoiding deceptive charting and ensuring accessibility

The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the data scientist at Lumen Mobile, a fictional phone carrier. Three churn models are in the experiment tracker; the retention team wants a recommendation today. Only 4% of customers churn each month.
handover: Model C reports 99% accuracy and 0.99 AUC; models A and B report about 0.78 AUC.
The retention team can call 2,000 customers a month.
howItWorks: The console shows the open dataset, its quality flags and a table of the checks and their results.
Move on a step at a time. A decision comes to you at each step; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Step 2: in a production dry run, C's predictions are near random because cancellation dates don't exist yet.
Step 3: the 'most accurate' model flags almost nobody; the retention team calls customers at random for a month.
Step 4: finance funds a large campaign expecting a big uplift; actual saves are a fraction of what the chart implied.

leakPrompt.title: Too good to be true
leakPrompt.context: Model C uses a feature that exists only after churn is decided.

choices.label: Remove features that exist only after the outcome, retrain C, and re-evaluate on a time-based holdout

effects.log: Without the leak, C scores 0.80 AUC.

choices.feedback: Target leakage inflates offline metrics and fails in production; a time-based holdout mirrors real use.

choices.label: Exclude model C and choose between A and B
choices.feedback: Safe, but C's other features might have been the best model.

choices.label: Recommend model C: the numbers are best
choices.feedback: In production the leaked feature doesn't exist yet when predictions are made; the model is useless.

choices.feedback: Accurate, but the director can't find the decision in it.

reflection.question: Write the recommendation: which model, the evidence that justifies it, and what it can't do.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Leak removed and time holdout; precision at 2,000 with a PR curve.
parts.modelAnswer: Model C leaked a post-churn feature; without it, on a time holdout, it scored 0.80. At the 2,000-call capacity, A's precision is 31%, C's 29%, B's 22%.

parts.label: Communication
parts.criteria: Expected saves, honest chart, limits and monitoring.
parts.modelAnswer: We recommend A, with expected saves at 31% precision, an honest lift chart, its limits and a monitoring plan.

scoring.modelReasoning: Justifying a model means evaluating it the way it will be used: features available at prediction time (no target leakage), a time-based holdout, and metrics that fit the imbalance and the business constraint (precision and recall at capacity, not accuracy). Recommendations to executives give the decision, the expected value and the limits, with charts that don't mislead.
